sources.name: Financial Statements of the Government of New Zealand for the Year Ended 30 June 2024 (Treasury B.11), 'Fiscal Indicator Analysis - Expenses by Functional Classification'
sources.assumptions: All functional-classification categories below (health, education, etc.) and Finance costs are Core Crown actuals for FY2024 (excludes Crown entities/SOEs, e.g. Kaainga Ora, health entities - matches the scope this project's revenue side already taxes). Core Crown total expenses (excl. losses) is $138,998m, which these categories sum to exactly - Finance costs ($8,943m) is NOT one of the OECD functional categories but Treasury includes it in this same table so the total ties out; omitting it would silently under-count by ~$8.9bn, the same class of gap already found and fixed in this project's otherIndirectResidual. Figures converted from $NZDm to $K by x1000.

sources.date: August 2025 (MSD Annual Report 2025, FY2024 comparative column)
sources.name: Ministry of Social Development Annual Report 2025 (G.60), 'Benefits or Related Expenses' note, p.182
sources.assumptions: NZ Superannuation ($21,574,368k), Jobseeker Support and Emergency Benefit combined ($4,062,221k - MSD does not separate these), Sole Parent Support ($2,097,032k), Supported Living Payment ($2,530,299k), Accommodation Assistance ($2,410,658k), and a residual 'Other Benefits or Related Expenses' line ($948,233k, which bundles the Winter Energy Payment with other unspecified benefits - WEP's own figure can't be isolated from this table) are all real MSD actuals. These six lines sum to $33,622,811k, well short of the Treasury functional 'Social security and welfare' total below ($44,589,000k) - the gap is other MSD/Vote items never itemised here (e.g. disability allowance, student allowance) plus Working for Families (see next source), not a data error. Modelled as an explicit 'welfareResidual' component rather than silently dropped, mirroring this project's otherIndirectResidual precedent.

sources.date: 3 September 2025 (data extract, 2024 tax year = year ended 31 March 2024)
sources.name: Inland Revenue - Working for Families statistics
sources.assumptions: Working for Families Tax Credits: $3,043m paid to 328,400 claiming families, 2024 tax year (year ended 31 March 2024 - IRD's tax-year convention, not the 30 June Crown fiscal year used everywhere else in this project, same kind of vintage mismatch already flagged for FBT/trust tax). Per this project's convention (tax credits/exemptions belong under the tax they offset, not under expenditure), WFF is NOT one of the expenditure components below - it's subtracted out of the 'welfareResidual' component here so it isn't double-counted (once as a credit reducing income tax, and again baked into the unmodelled welfare residual), and is intended to be modelled as a credit against income tax revenue instead. The 2025 tax year figure isn't published yet as of this extract - both FY2024 and FY2025 expenditure files reuse this same 2024-tax-year figure for the subtraction, flagged as an approximation.

sources.name: MSD Benefit Fact Sheets Snapshot, June 2024 Quarter
sources.assumptions: Recipient counts as at end of June 2024: Jobseeker Support 196,434; Sole Parent Support 76,959; Supported Living Payment 103,152. Used to back-derive each benefit's real $/year/recipient rate (spend / recipients) below, the same back-derivation technique already used elsewhere in this project (e.g. cgt/land/fbt base-from-revenue). NZ Superannuation recipient counts are not published in this text-extractable Snapshot table (MSD's NZS/Veteran's Pension client counts are Excel-only) - a genuine gap, not resolved here.

sources.name: Stats NZ - 'One million people aged 65+ by 2028'
sources.assumptions: 828,600 people aged 65+ (2023) is the only reasonably confirmed 65+ population figure found - used as a proxy for NZ Superannuation recipients (NZS is universal/non-means-tested for eligible residents 65+, so this is a reasonable stand-in, same technique as general.json's 15+ working-age proxy for UBI). Held flat across both FY2024 and FY2025 in this dataset since no separate per-year figure was obtainable via available tools - understates the true count given the growing 65+ cohort (Stats NZ projects 1 million by 2029), so the resulting $/year/recipient rate is itself an overestimate. A genuine precision gap, flagged rather than guessed at finer resolution.

sources.date: 30 October 2025 (release covering year ended 30 June 2024 comparative)
sources.name: Stats NZ - National population estimates: At 30 June 2024 (2018-base)
sources.assumptions: 5,338,500 - New Zealand's estimated resident population at 30 June 2024, on Stats NZ's then-current 2018-Census base. Used as the denominator for every 'direct spend' functional category's $/capita/year rate below (health, education, etc.) - this is a genuine real unit, not an abstract %-of-baseline. Flagged precision caveat: the FY2025 population figure (see that year's file) appears to be on a newer, post-2023-Census rebase, and the two headline figures imply a small population *decrease* year-on-year that is more likely a base-methodology artifact than real - not independently resolved in this pass since Stats NZ's release pages could not be fetched in full (JS-rendered), only search-summarised.

sources.name: Stats NZ - Government finance statistics (general government): Year ended June 2025 (nominal expenditure GDP)
sources.assumptions: Nominal GDP $420,100m (year ended June 2024) used only for the informational 'defence as % of GDP' readout in meta, not for any expenditure calculation. Moderate confidence only - obtained via search-tool summarisation, not a direct fetch of the release tables. Also note: this FSGNZ-derived 'Defence' functional-expense figure ($3,163m, 0.75% of this GDP figure) is Core Crown *operating expenses* only - it is NOT the same thing as the internationally-reported ~1.19%-of-GDP 'defence spending' figure (SIPRI/World Bank series) that the real-world '2% of GDP' political target refers to, which likely includes capital/acquisition spending and a different Vote-level scope. Don't conflate the two - the %-of-GDP shown against this dataset's defence category will read much lower than the political target for that reason, not because of a data error.
